readerTitle: Where 71% of fast-growing founders found their idea
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Amar Bhidé의 Inc. 500 창업자 인터뷰) + 가상 사례 (물류 창고, 소프트웨어 회사)
insight: 좋은 사업 아이디어는 머리를 짜내 발명하기보다, 이미 잘 아는 일 속에서 반복되는 문제를 알아차려서 얻는다.
misconception: 좋은 아이디어는 번뜩이는 영감이나 브레인스토밍에서 나오고, 세상에 없던 완전히 새로운 것이어야 한다.

sources.text: Bhidé, A. (1994). How Entrepreneurs Craft Strategies That Work. Harvard Business Review, March–April 1994.
Bhidé, A. (2000). The Origin and Evolution of New Businesses. Oxford University Press.
Graham, P. (2012). How to Get Startup Ideas. paulgraham.com (카드에는 직접 인용 없이 요지만 사용)

factChecks.note: "Inc. 500 창업자의 71%가 이전 직장에서 접한 아이디어를 그대로 쓰거나 변형했다"는 수치가 Bhidé(1994) HBR 논문의 표현과 일치하는지 원문으로 확인하세요. 표본(1989년 Inc. 500 기업 창업자 약 100명 인터뷰)과 연도도 함께 확인이 필요합니다.
차트의 '다른 출처 29%'는 100% − 71%로 계산한 값입니다. 원문에 다른 범주(우연히 발견 등)의 세부 비율이 있으면 그것으로 바꾸지 말고 합계 기준으로만 표시하세요.
Paul Graham 에세이의 요지(아이디어를 '생각해 내려' 하지 말고 문제, 특히 자기 자신이 겪는 문제를 찾아라)를 원문과 대조해 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용하지 않고 바꿔 썼습니다.
창고, 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 모두 설명용 가상 사례입니다.

cards.title: Where 71% of fast-growing founders found their idea
body: Picture the moment a business idea is born. Maybe a late night, a whiteboard, a flash of genius.
When a researcher asked founders of fast-growing US companies where their ideas came from, the most common answer was much less dramatic. It was their old job.

image.label: A lightbulb sitting on an ordinary office desk next to a time card
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 평범한 사무실 책상 위에 출근 카드, 커피잔, 서류 더미가 있고 그 사이에 작은 전구가 조용히 켜져 있음. 극적인 번개 효과 없이 일상적인 분위기. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Three would-be founders. Whose idea would you bet on?
body: Each wants to start a business this year. You can back only one.
Whose idea is most likely to turn into something real?

options.text: A designer who spent a weekend listing hot trends and picked the most exciting one
options.feedback: Trend lists make ideas that sound big. But she doesn't know who has the problem, how bad it is, or what they use today.

options.text: A warehouse supervisor who fixed the same pallet-labeling mistakes every week for six years
options.feedback: He knows the problem, what it costs, and who pays for the fix. The idea is less exciting, but it rests on years of evidence.

options.text: A consultant who saw one client struggle with shipping delays
options.feedback: A real problem seen up close is a good start. One sighting, though, can't tell her if it's common or a one-off.

cards.title: Most ideas came from work, not inspiration.
body: In a study published in 1994, Amar Bhidé interviewed founders of Inc. 500 companies, a list of fast-growing US firms.
**71%** had copied or changed an idea they ran into at a previous job.

groups.label: Where Inc. 500 founders got their idea

rows.label: Copied or changed an idea from a previous job

cards.title: Good ideas are noticed, not invented.
body: Most workable business ideas come from **close, repeated contact with a problem**. Usually that contact happens at work, where you see the same pain week after week.

The warehouse supervisor didn't think up his idea. He lived next to it until he couldn't ignore it. Writer and investor Paul Graham made a similar point in 2012: stop trying to think of ideas, and look for problems, ideally your own.

image.label: A magnifying glass over a repeated mistake on a work checklist
image.brief: 인포그래픽 스타일. 업무 체크리스트에 같은 실수 표시(빨간 X)가 매주 반복되고, 돋보기가 그 반복 패턴을 비추고 있음. 옆에 작은 라벨 "Noticed, not invented". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why insiders see ideas others miss.
body: Time inside a problem gives you facts no brainstorm can. Look for these signs where you already work:
list: **Workarounds:** a spreadsheet, sticky note or manual step everyone uses to patch a gap
**Repeat complaints:** customers or coworkers raising the same issue again and again
**Paid by hand:** work people pay someone to do slowly that could be done better
**Ideas from next door:** something that works in one market but is missing in yours
cards.callout: The best ideas often look boring from outside. That keeps rivals away.

cards.title: Original isn't the point.
body: Notice the word *changed* in that 71%. Many founders didn't create anything new. They took a known business to a new city, a new customer, or did it with fewer errors.
A bakery owner who sees a wholesale supplier in another region serving cafés well can bring the same model home. A good idea needs to fit a real problem, not to be the first of its kind.

cards.title: Being close to a problem has blind spots.
body: Your problem may be yours alone. Six years of pallet errors could reflect one badly run warehouse, not an industry.
Insiders can also stop seeing what outsiders find obvious, or assume the old way of doing things is the only way.
Noticing a problem is where an idea starts, not proof it's worth building. Checking that others share it comes next.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You're a product manager planning to leave and start a business. You have three ideas. Which one has the strongest source?

options.text: A booking app for dental clinics, after a podcast called the market huge
options.feedback: Big market, but you've never worked with a dental clinic. You'd be guessing at their problems from the outside.

options.text: A tool like the one your team hacked together to clean messy customer data, a job your team handled by hand every week
options.feedback: You've lived the problem, built a rough fix, and know what it saves. Next you'd check that other companies have the same mess.

options.text: A new social app, because you're tired of the existing ones
options.feedback: Personal frustration is a real source. But a mood about apps is vaguer than a weekly task you know in detail.

cards.title: Look at your own work before you look for genius.
body: Most strong ideas come from problems you've seen over and over, not from a blank page.
**Try it today:** write down three workarounds you or your team use every week. Next to each, note who else might have the same problem.
